A씨는 신입사원에게 작성 방법을 알려줬지만, 다음 날 확인해 보니 서명만 남아 있고 점검 항목 상당수가 비어 있었다.A씨가 누락된 부분을 지적하자 신입사원은 표정이 굳은 채 대답했고, 이후 하루 동안 A씨에게 말을 걸지 않았다고 한다. 다른 선배들과는 웃으며 대화하다가 A씨가 휴게실에 들어서자 조용해지는 모습도 보였다고 전했다.문제는 비슷한 일이 다음 주에도 반복됐다는 것이다. articles.title: I’ve debated with Israel’s most fervent defenders – NAZA debunks their talking points | Mehdi Hasan
articles.snippet: The film’s testimonies from Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers expose years of baseless propaganda. Don’t take my word – take theirs I watched the extraordinary new Guardian-produced documentary from Oscar-winning Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor the other night, and I have struggled to stop thinking about it ever since. The film’s title comes from a Hebrew military term for collateral damage, and it consists of eye-opening interviews with two dozen Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers sitting in darkness, often on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, their voices “digitally altered to disguise their identities”. articles.title: An open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to Trainspotting
articles.snippet: Not every great novel makes a great movie, and sometimes the opposite is true. But regardless of the source text, or how beloved characters are treated, there is more than one way to write a successful adaptation It is always fun to join in a craze, like a Victorian going mad for penny farthings. Which is probably why, against my better judgment, I went to see Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster The Odyssey this summer, buying my ticket into the popular conversation along with everyone else. This year’s other divisive adaptation, Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights, had the world and his wife arguing about it before they had even watched the film. No doubt the makers of the recent Sense and Sensibility movie were also hoping for lots of people to go and see it to discover whether they hated it. After all, very few of us leave the cinema saying: “That’s exactly how I pictured it in my head.” Or even less likely: “That was better than the book.” We’re more likely to shake our fists at how they ruined the ending, dumbed it down, unforgivably cast somebody with the wrong hair, or betrayed a beloved character, as with last year’s Thursday Murder Club debacle.
